content: Actinic cheilitis, also referred to as actinic cheilosis or sailor's lip, is a condition that represents the lip counterpart of actinic keratosis of the skin. It has the potential to progress into squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). This condition is characterized by a thickened, whitish discoloration of the lip, particularly at the junction between the lip and the surrounding skin. The normally well-defined vermillion border, which separates the red lip tissue from the adjacent skin, becomes blurred or lost. As the condition advances, the affected lip may develop a scaly texture and become indurated (hardened). Actinic cheilitis is typically painless and persistent. Additional contributing factors may include tobacco use, irritation of the lips, poor oral hygiene, and the use of ill-fitting dentures. Actinic cheilitis is considered a premalignant condition, as approximately 10% of cases may progress to squamous cell carcinoma. Since it is not possible to predict which lesions will become malignant, the standard recommendation is to treat all cases. Treatment options aim to destroy or remove the damaged epithelium and include the use of topical medications, surgical procedures, and other interventions. Common treatments include 5-fluorouracil (5-FU), imiquimod, scalpel vermillionectomy, chemical peeling, electrosurgery, and carbon dioxide laser vaporization. While these treatments are generally effective, they are associated with varying degrees of pain, swelling, and a low recurrence rate. Topical 5-fluorouracil (5-FU), marketed under names such as Efudex and Carac, is an effective treatment for diffuse but mild cases of actinic cheilitis. This medication works by inhibiting DNA synthesis, which disproportionately affects rapidly dividing cells, leading to their destruction. Normal skin cells are less affected. Treatment typically lasts 2 to 4 weeks, depending on the patient’s response. The treatment process involves an inflammatory phase, followed by redness, burning, oozing, and eventual erosion of the affected area. Therapy is discontinued once ulceration and crusting develop. Scarring is minimal, and complete clearance of the condition has been reported in approximately 50% of patients. Imiquimod (Aldara) is another topical treatment that acts as an immune response modifier. It stimulates the immune system to target and destroy abnormal cells, leading to apoptosis (programmed cell death) of tumor cells. Imiquimod induces macrophage infiltration into the epidermis, resulting in erosion of the affected tissue, and activates T-cells to enhance the immune response. This treatment may also promote an immune memory, reducing the likelihood of lesion recurrence. Scarring is minimal, and complete clearance has been observed in up to 45% of patients with actinic keratoses. However, the optimal dosage, duration of therapy, and long-term efficacy for actinic cheilitis remain under investigation. For smaller areas of actinic cheilitis, cryosurgery and electrosurgery are effective treatment options. Cryosurgery involves the application of liquid nitrogen using an open spray technique. Local anesthesia is not typically required, but treating the entire lip can be painful. Cure rates exceeding 96% have been reported, making cryosurgery the preferred treatment for localized lesions. Electrosurgery, which requires local anesthesia, is an alternative but is less practical due to the need for anesthesia. Both techniques may cause damage to adjacent tissues, potentially delaying healing and increasing the risk of scarring. For more extensive or recurrent cases, surgical procedures such as shave vermillionectomy or carbon dioxide laser ablation may be employed. A shave vermillionectomy involves the removal of a portion of the vermillion ridge while preserving the underlying muscle. This procedure can result in significant bleeding due to the vascular nature of the lip, and a linear scar may form. However, scarring can often be minimized with massage and steroid therapy. Healing is typically rapid, and the procedure is highly effective. Carbon dioxide laser ablation is another option, which involves the precise removal of the affected tissue. This technique requires a skilled operator and usually necessitates anesthesia. While secondary infections and scarring are possible, these complications are generally minimal and respond well to steroid treatment. Pain during the healing phase can persist for three weeks or longer. Despite these challenges, carbon dioxide laser ablation has a high success rate with minimal recurrence. Chemical peeling using 50% trichloroacetic acid has also been evaluated as a treatment for actinic cheilitis. Healing typically occurs within 7 to 10 days, and side effects are minimal. However, studies suggest that the success rate of this method may be less than 30%, making it a less favorable option compared to other treatments.
